title: Adult epimorphic regeneration of a functional limb

concept.text: The innovation would be a controllable biological program that allows an adult mammal, ultimately a human, to regrow a functional digit or limb after amputation. Epimorphic regeneration means rebuilding the missing structures through a blastema: a localized population of responding cells that grows and forms replacement tissues. Success would require restoring the correct anatomy for the amputation level, including skeleton, joints, muscle, tendons, skin, blood supply and peripheral nerves, with useful sensation and movement.

Adult mammalian limb and proximal digit amputations generally heal by fibrosis rather than replacing the missing appendage. Endogenous epimorphic regeneration in this context is largely restricted to distal digit tips. The proposed advance would extend that restricted response by forming a blastema, respecifying positional identity—how cells determine which structures belong at a particular location—and coordinating replacement of the patterned tissues beyond an adult amputation plane. A complete functional digit would be an important intermediate milestone toward the broader limb goal.

significance.text: If achieved, this capability would allow anatomy lost through injury to be rebuilt from the person's living tissues, with sensation and motion appropriate to the amputation level. Its revolutionary consequence would be biological restoration of a coordinated appendage: replacement tissues would have to form a working anatomical system. The reported ability of neonatal mouse stump cells to contribute to new skeletal and connective structures provides a technical basis for this possibility, but does not demonstrate adult functional limb regeneration.

Conditional downstream possibilities include regeneration after amputations required by infection or cancer. Those applications would also need evidence that the underlying disease is controlled and that regeneration is safe in the affected tissue environment. Congenital transverse deficiency presents an additional problem: initiating the appropriate pattern without an injury-created stump or an embryonic limb bud. These are proposed extensions of the capability, not established consequences of the reported experiments.

A regenerated arm with fine hand control, normal proprioception and appropriate growth would demand more than recognizable anatomy. It would require sufficiently specific nerve connections, coordinated muscle forces, mechanically competent joints and control of size and growth. The partial neonatal digit anatomy and adult digit bone repair described in the supplied evidence do not establish those capabilities. Spinal-cord reconnection is a separate problem and is outside this concept.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability is reliable induction and control of adult appendage regeneration beyond naturally regenerative digit-tip levels. Forming a blastema is one component; the cells must also acquire the positional identities needed to replace the structures actually removed. Growth without correct pattern could yield elongated bone or an incomplete skeletal element without reconstructing a digit, wrist or hand. The neonatal mouse results connect blastema formation and positional respecification to induced skeletal regeneration, while leaving adult applicability unresolved.

The wound environment is another barrier. The supplied Mui study associates regenerative mouse digit wounds with a softer, hyaluronic-acid-rich environment and nonregenerative wounds with dense collagen and greater stiffness. HAPLN1 interventions reduced scarring and enhanced bone repair in the tested adult setting. The missing step is converting such permissive repair conditions into sustained, correctly patterned regeneration of all required tissues; improved extracellular matrix conditions alone have not demonstrated that outcome.

Engineering synthesis: an adult-scale program would need to coordinate vascular supply, skeletal growth, joint surfaces, tendon and ligament attachments, muscle restoration, skin coverage and nerve integration over a much larger volume than a neonatal mouse digit. It would also need to stop growth at the appropriate size and maintain stable tissue identities. The challenge is therefore both spatial and temporal: the correct tissues must develop in the correct relationships and become mechanically and neurologically integrated with the retained limb.

Functional integration remains a distinct barrier even when joint-like anatomy appears. The Yu peer-review record explicitly distinguishes anatomical evidence of synovial joint regeneration from functional characterization. Demonstrating a joint cavity or connective-tissue attachment does not establish load-bearing performance, active movement, protective sensation or coordinated use.

current_state.text: Yu and colleagues reported on 17 April 2026 in Nature Communications, volume 17, article 5346, that sequential FGF2 followed by BMP2 treatment induced a blastema-mediated regenerative response after a normally nonregenerative mouse digit amputation. The experiments used hindlimb digits 2 and 4 at postnatal day 3, amputated midway through the second phalanx, P2. The response included an imperfect P3-like skeletal element—resembling the terminal phalanx—and a separate joint-like response with tendon and ligament attachments. This was a neonatal digit model, not an adult limb experiment.

The identity and completeness of the regenerated anatomy require careful wording. The reported elements were variable and included P3-like and sesamoid-like structures; restoration of P2 remained below age-matched controls. In the supplied peer-review record, the authors adopted the more cautious P3-like and sesamoid-like terminology and acknowledged that their joint evidence was anatomical. Functional joint performance was not established. The earlier reviewer concerns support this narrower interpretation; they do not independently negate the reported anatomical response.

Mui and colleagues reported on 9 April 2026 in Science, doi:10.1126/science.ady3136, that regenerative mouse digit wounds were softer and enriched in hyaluronic acid, whereas nonregenerative wounds contained dense collagen. The retained author manuscript provides more than an abstract: it describes HAPLN1 interventions, including transplantation of HAPLN1-overexpressing fibroblasts after nonregenerative amputations in adult immunocompromised mice. The reported outcomes included reduced scarring, partial restoration and enhanced bone repair or elongation. These results extend the evidence to an adult experimental setting, but do not establish complete functional digit regeneration or performance in an intact immune context.

Scientific American's 9 April 2026 account describes work by Tsissios and colleagues using low oxygen in embryonic mouse tissue to activate early regenerative responses. It also states that neither of the two Science studies regrew entire mammalian limbs. The reconciled research attributes rapid wound healing after reduced oxygen or HIF1A stabilization to the Tsissios paper, doi:10.1126/science.adw8526, and describes a comparison with frog tadpole limbs. However, the primary paper was not captured in the supplied evidence, so those exact experimental details and the specific HIF1A claim remain unverified here. The secondary account supports an early-response interpretation, not a claim of mammalian limb regrowth.

Two additional reports appear in the reconciled research but lack retained documents in the supplied review: a Lab Animal summary by Le Bras dated 5 May 2026, doi:10.1038/s41684-026-01735-4, described as identifying the mouse tissue as cultured explants, and an 8 October 2026 Development review by Sammarco and McCusker, 153(19):dev205585, described as reiterating the restriction of mammalian regeneration largely to distal digit tips. The research reports purchase-wall access for the Development full text. Their exact wording and scope cannot be confirmed from the supplied review; their absence is an evidence limitation, not evidence that their reported conclusions are false.

The supplied review assessed the full main-article text and peer-review record for Yu, the retained main author manuscript for Mui, and the Scientific American account. It did not visually inspect Yu's figures or inspect Mui's original images and supplementary methods. Two indexed Yu supplementary PDFs also had pages without extractable text, so their presence in the source index does not establish assessment of their visual contents. These limitations constrain interpretation of detailed anatomy and methods without overturning the narrower textual findings.

Within this evidence set, the demonstrated advances are induced, imperfect neonatal digit anatomy and adult digit scar modulation with enhanced bone repair. Adult-scale, fully patterned regeneration with integrated innervation and useful function remains unresolved. The supplied freshness record is empty, so these dated findings cannot establish a comprehensive account of the field through 1 November 2026.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed intermediate demonstration: following amputation proximal to the nail organ, an adult mammal at least as large as a pig regenerates a complete digit with an anatomically appropriate joint, tendon, bone, nail or equivalent protective cover, protective sensation and active movement. The result should remain functional for at least two years without a permanent implant, followed by convincing human demonstration. Pig-scale testing and two-year durability are proposed thresholds for this record, not established scientific or clinical standards.
completion_criteria.label: Two-year functional digit regeneration in pig-scale mammals, then humans

completion_criteria.text: Proposed limb-level demonstration: regeneration distal to a forearm amputation restores the missing forearm tissues, wrist and hand, with useful mechanical and neurological integration at the retained elbow. A forearm-level amputation ordinarily preserves the elbow; regeneration of the elbow itself would require a separate demonstration after a more proximal amputation. Completing the digit milestone alone would not complete the whole-limb innovation.
completion_criteria.label: Forearm-level regeneration restores the hand with functional elbow integration

completion_criteria.text: Proposed functional assessment should combine anatomical imaging and tissue examination with evidence of load-bearing capacity, joint stability and movement, active force generation, sensory protection and coordinated use. Histology alone, a skeletal spike or a joint-like structure without demonstrated performance would not meet these criteria. This requirement addresses the distinction between anatomical and functional regeneration explicitly acknowledged in the Yu peer-review record.
completion_criteria.label: Anatomical and performance assessments demonstrate load-bearing capacity and coordinated use

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: independent groups should reproduce the outcome using defined treatments, appropriate controls and transparent reporting of success rates, anatomical variation, adverse outcomes and durability. Demonstrations should identify the tested ages, amputation levels, immune conditions and tissue environments, including whether treatment depends on immunosuppression. Long-term assessment should examine growth control, mechanical failure, abnormal tissue formation, pain and loss of function. A finite set of successful experiments would establish the breadth actually demonstrated; it would not prove regeneration at every amputation level or in every patient.
completion_criteria.label: Independent reproduction reports treatment outcomes, durability and tested biological boundaries

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis — ORT-02, Biological restoration of the osteoarthritic synovial joint: limb regeneration would need functional new joints, creating overlap in cartilage, synovial organization and joint mechanics. ORT-02 addresses restoration of an existing diseased joint, whereas ORT-01 requires formation of joints within missing anatomy. A joint-like response in a neonatal digit completes neither concept.

Roster-based synthesis — ORT-03, Eradication of mature biofilm in bone and on orthopedic implants without removing the reconstruction: infection control could enable regeneration in previously infected tissues, but eliminating biofilm is distinct from inducing a patterned appendage. Successful regeneration would not by itself demonstrate eradication of infection, and successful biofilm treatment would not demonstrate regenerative capacity.

Roster-based synthesis — ORT-04, Regeneration of the load-bearing tendon–bone enthesis: a functional regenerated limb would require durable transfer of force from tendons into bone. ORT-04 isolates that attachment problem. Anatomical tendon or ligament attachment in the Yu response does not establish the mature load-bearing performance required for either an enthesis restoration claim or a functional limb.

Roster-based synthesis — ORT-05, Restoration of the intervertebral disc as a living load-bearing organ: both concepts involve coordinated tissue organization and durable mechanical function. Disc restoration concerns a specialized axial organ; it does not require the positional program that reconstructs an appendage beyond an amputation plane.

Roster-based synthesis — ORT-06, Force-bearing skeletal muscle after volumetric muscle loss: restoring muscle mass, architecture, force and innervation would be a major component of proximal limb regeneration. ORT-06 addresses a muscle deficit within retained anatomy, while ORT-01 must coordinate muscle with newly patterned bones, joints, attachments, vessels and skin.

Roster-based synthesis — ORT-07, Meaningful motor and sensory recovery across long peripheral-nerve gaps: nerve extension and appropriate target reconnection overlap directly with the sensory and motor requirements of a regenerated limb. ORT-07 concerns recovery across nerve gaps; ORT-01 additionally requires creation of the missing anatomical targets and their integration. Neither concept includes spinal-cord reconnection.

Roster-based synthesis — ORT-08, Anatomically precise and reversible control of osteogenesis: spatial control of bone formation would support correct skeletal pattern and growth termination in regeneration. ORT-08 isolates control of osteogenesis. Bone elongation or a newly formed skeletal element is an enabling result, not completion of a multitissue functional appendage.

Roster-based synthesis — ORT-09, Regeneration of a functioning growth plate: a functioning growth plate could become relevant if a regenerated limb must grow appropriately during childhood. Adult limb regeneration and restoration of longitudinal growth are distinct achievements; a successful adult demonstration would not establish pediatric growth capacity.

Roster-based synthesis — ORT-10, Single-episode restoration of segmental long bone by vascularized, remodelable bone: both concepts require viable skeletal tissue that integrates and tolerates load. ORT-10 reconstructs a bone segment within retained limb anatomy. ORT-01 must also determine and rebuild the missing distal pattern, including joints and other tissues.

change_log.change: Qualified the fibrosis statement and restricted the digit-tip limitation to mammalian appendage regeneration.
change_log.reason: The supplied evidence supports a general amputation response, not a universal statement about all mammalian wounds or all forms of multitissue regeneration.

change_log.change: Integrated blastema formation, positional respecification and coordinated functional tissue restoration into the concept and remaining barriers.
change_log.reason: The useful mechanistic detail explains why wound closure, bone growth and complete appendage regeneration are distinct achievements.

change_log.change: Replaced definitive distal-phalanx restoration language with imperfect P3-like and sesamoid-like anatomy, and preserved incomplete P2 restoration and unestablished joint function.
change_log.reason: The validated review and author responses support cautious anatomical terminology without rejecting the narrower reported response.

change_log.change: Added the postnatal-day-3, hindlimb-digit and mid-P2 details of the Yu experiments.
change_log.reason: These details define the demonstrated age and amputation scope and prevent extrapolation to adult limbs.

change_log.change: Corrected Mui's evidence description from abstract-only access to a retained main author manuscript and included the adult immunocompromised model and HAPLN1 intervention.
change_log.reason: The reviewed manuscript supports more experimental detail than the candidate acknowledged, while still demonstrating repair rather than complete functional digit regeneration.

change_log.change: Separated the secondary account of Tsissios from unverified primary HIF1A and experimental details, and retained the Lab Animal and October Development reports with explicit access limitations.
change_log.reason: The missing documents prevent confirmation of exact claims; they do not establish that those claims are false.

change_log.change: Removed unsupported categorical statements about present clinical outcomes and transplant immunosuppression; retained the conditional regenerative impact.
change_log.reason: The supplied sources do not establish those clinical assertions, and the central significance does not depend on them.

change_log.change: Made infection, cancer, congenital deficiency, fine control, proprioception and childhood growth conditional extensions requiring additional demonstrations.
change_log.reason: The reported experimental results do not establish these applications or capabilities.

change_log.change: Corrected the forearm/elbow anatomy and distinguished complete-digit milestones from completion of limb regeneration.
change_log.reason: A forearm amputation ordinarily retains the elbow; elbow regeneration requires a more proximal test.

change_log.change: Identified large-animal size and two-year durability as proposed thresholds and added reproducibility, functional assessment and demonstrated-scope boundaries.
change_log.reason: The candidate's thresholds are not published standards, and anatomical appearance alone cannot establish durable function.

change_log.change: Preserved image, supplementary-extraction and freshness limitations and mapped all nine other roster concepts without merging them.
change_log.reason: The record must reflect the actual evidence reviewed and preserve distinctions between enabling capabilities and whole-appendage regeneration.

unresolved_issues: The exact Tsissios primary findings, including the HIF1A intervention, comparison with frog tadpole limbs and experimental tissue preparation, remain unverified because the primary document was not captured.

The cited Lab Animal summary and October Development review were absent from the supplied evidence; their exact wording, scope and the reported Development access restriction cannot be independently confirmed from this review.
The supplied freshness record is empty, so the evidence does not establish a comprehensive state-of-field assessment through 1 November 2026.

Yu's anatomical findings were assessed through text and peer-review responses without visual inspection of figures. Poorly extractable supplementary PDFs do not resolve the remaining visual-evidence limitations.
Mui's supplementary methods and original images were not inspected; the generalizability of the reported adult immunocompromised-mouse response to an intact immune setting remains unresolved.
The supplied studies do not establish durable functional joint performance, complete adult digit regeneration, adult limb-scale patterning or human translation.
Disease-specific safety, congenital initiation, fine hand control, proprioception and childhood growth remain additional application questions.
The proposed pig-scale and two-year criteria require future justification and refinement; they are retained as explicit proposals rather than consensus thresholds.

prerequisites.reason: A regenerated limb needs load-bearing tendon–bone attachments to transfer muscle force into its skeleton.
A regenerated limb needs living, innervated skeletal muscle that produces voluntary force.
A regenerated limb needs peripheral nerves to reach distant targets and restore useful movement and protective sensation.
